children.text: Chapter 15's first objection ends with a list of what the existing oversight arrangements do not provide, and earned-value tracking is on it. The book's point is that monthly reports track activities, not performance. They say what was done, not whether the work is delivering the value planned for the money and time spent.

Earned value management (EVM) is the standard technique for measuring performance in that sense. This lesson explains its three core quantities and four basic indicators, works through an illustrative example, sets out the federal standards that govern it, and then marks its limits: what EVM cannot tell a five-pillar portfolio manager, and what has to be read alongside it.
EVM is most useful for predictive components with a baseline. For adaptive components, Lesson 8's cycle-output measures fit better. A portfolio office uses each where it fits.
The Three Core Quantities

Earned value compares three numbers at any point in time. Planned value (PV) is the budgeted cost of the work scheduled to be done by now. Earned value (EV) is the budgeted cost of the work actually completed by now. Actual cost (AC) is what has really been spent to complete that work.

The insight of EVM is that progress is measured in the budget's own units. A component that has spent half its money has not necessarily done half its work; earned value asks how much of the planned work, valued at its planned cost, is genuinely complete. Comparing earned value with planned value shows whether the component is ahead of or behind schedule. Comparing earned value with actual cost shows whether it is over or under budget for the work done.

EVM depends on a baseline: a scope broken into measurable pieces, each with a planned cost and a planned date. That is why it fits predictive components and why the book's finding that no pillar has a formal work-breakdown structure (Lesson 6) matters. Without a baseline there is nothing to earn value against.

Planned value is what you said you would have done. Earned value is what you have actually done, valued at plan. Actual cost is what it really cost. Every EVM indicator is a comparison of two of these three numbers.
Four Basic Indicators

Schedule variance is earned value minus planned value: negative means less work is done than planned. Cost variance is earned value minus actual cost: negative means the work done cost more than planned. The two performance indices express the same comparisons as ratios. The schedule performance index (SPI) is earned value divided by planned value, and the cost performance index (CPI) is earned value divided by actual cost. A value of 1.0 means on plan; below 1.0 means behind schedule or over cost.

Ratios are useful at portfolio level because they let components of very different sizes be compared on one scale. A component with an SPI of 0.8 is delivering eighty percent of its planned work rate, whether its budget is two hundred thousand dollars or twenty million.

The indices also support forecasting. If a component's cost performance has been stable, dividing its total budget by its CPI gives a rough estimate at completion. Forecasts like this are only as good as the stability of past performance, but they are far more informative than a status of 'in progress'.

children.text: An Illustrative Calculation

Consider a hypothetical analytics deployment with a total budget of $2.0 million. These figures are invented to show the arithmetic; they are not Vermont's. Six months in, the plan said $1.0 million of work would be complete, so planned value is $1.0 million. Measured against the work breakdown, the work actually finished was budgeted at $0.8 million, so earned value is $0.8 million. Actual spending to date is $1.0 million.

Schedule variance is $0.8 million minus $1.0 million, or minus $0.2 million, and the SPI is 0.8: the component has delivered eighty percent of the work it planned to deliver by now. Cost variance is $0.8 million minus $1.0 million, also minus $0.2 million, and the CPI is 0.8: each dollar spent has bought eighty cents of planned work. If that cost performance holds, the simple estimate at completion is $2.0 million divided by 0.8, or $2.5 million.

A monthly activity report for the same component might read 'vendor onboarded, data feeds in testing, on track for go-live'. Both can be true at once. The earned-value view shows what the activity view hides: the component is behind and over cost, and the gap will grow unless something changes.

children.text: Federal Standards and Expectations

Earned value is not an exotic private-sector technique; it is embedded in federal practice. The Government Accountability Office's Cost Estimating and Assessment Guide (GAO-20-195G), issued in March 2020 as the first update to its 2009 guide, sets out best practices for managing program cost through earned value management, including how an EVM system is set up, executed and validated. Federal agencies implement EVM systems against the industry guidelines in the EIA-748 standard.

This matters for a state transformation funded partly by federal programs. Federal partners and auditors are used to performance measured this way, and a portfolio office that can report schedule and cost performance indices for its major components speaks their language. Chapter 15's second objection makes the related point that a time-bounded, outcome-specified, heavily financed portfolio with legally binding deadlines is exactly the kind of work that federal partners expect to be professionally managed.

A state need not adopt a full certified EVM system to benefit. Applying the core quantities to the handful of large predictive components, with a simple monthly calculation, captures most of the value at little cost.
Start small: the three or four largest predictive components, a baseline for each, and a monthly SPI and CPI. That alone turns an activity report into a performance report.
What Earned Value Cannot See

Earned value measures adherence to plan. It cannot tell whether the plan respects the portfolio's dependencies. A component can report an SPI of 1.0, perfectly on schedule, while it is running ahead of its upstream gate and producing output nobody can yet use. In the terms of Lesson 7, earned value would score such a component as healthy while the sequencing test flags it as a problem.

Nor does earned value measure benefits. A component can be delivered on time and on budget and still fail to produce the benefit that justified it, which is why Track 4 adds benefits-realization tracking. And for adaptive components, whose plans are meant to change, a fixed baseline is the wrong yardstick altogether.

The portfolio office therefore reads three things together each month: earned value for the predictive components, the sequencing verdicts for every component, and benefits indicators against the goals the portfolio serves. Each catches failures the others miss.
